items.stem: Roughly how does the diameter of a nucleus compare with the diameter of the atom?
items.answer: About 100 000 times smaller
items.markingKey: About 100 000 times smaller. ~10⁻¹⁵ m vs ~10⁻¹⁰ m.

items.stem: Distinguish between the plum-pudding model and the nuclear model.
items.answer: The plum-pudding model spreads positive charge throughout the atom with electrons embedded; the nuclear model puts the positive charge and mass in a tiny central nucleus with electrons around it.
items.markingKey: The plum-pudding model spreads positive charge throughout the atom with electrons embedded; the nuclear model puts the positive charge and mass in a tiny central nucleus with electrons around it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "Isotopes of an element have different numbers of protons." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Isotopes have the same number of protons; only the number of neutrons differs.
items.markingKey: Isotopes have the same number of protons; only the number of neutrons differs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Sofia used a simulation of the gold-foil experiment and recorded alpha-particle counts per minute at different scattering angles (three runs).

Scattering angle / ° | Count rate / counts/min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
15 | 4066 | 3956 | 4114
30 | 262 | 251 | 258
45 | 52 | 54 | 54
60 | 19 | 19 | 18
90 | 5 | 4 | 4

Calculate the mean count rate when the scattering angle was 60 °.
items.answer: 18.7 counts/min
items.markingKey: M1 (19 + 19 + 18) ÷ 3; A1 18.7 counts/min (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Sana plans to investigate how the angle of deflection affects the number of alpha particles detected, using a computer simulation of the gold-foil experiment. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same simulated foil thickness; the same alpha-particle energy; the same counting time; the same target element (gold)
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: the same simulated foil thickness – thicker foil gives more scattering; the same alpha-particle energy – faster particles are deflected less; the same counting time – longer times give larger counts; the same target element (gold) – nuclear charge affects deflection. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The alpha-scattering experiment proved that the plum-pudding model was completely wrong."
items.answer: The experiment disproved the distribution of charge in the plum-pudding model, but science builds on earlier models rather than discarding them completely.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large-angle deflections could not happen with spread-out charge; the results fitted a nuclear model quantitatively. Arguments against: the model correctly included electrons and overall neutrality; one experiment led to a better model, which was itself later refined (Bohr, neutrons). Supported judgement: The experiment disproved the distribution of charge in the plum-pudding model, but science builds on earlier models rather than discarding them completely.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "atomic number (Z)"?
options: Radiation that can knock electrons out of atoms, forming ions
Using the known half-life of an isotope to find the age of a rock or once-living material
Exposing an object to radiation; it does not make the object radioactive
The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element
items.answer: The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element
items.markingKey: D. "atomic number (Z)" is the number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the element.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a few alpha particles were deflected through large angles.
items.answer: They passed very close to a nucleus, and the strong repulsion between the positive alpha particle and the positive nucleus pushed them sharply away.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They passed very close to a nucleus, and the strong repulsion between the positive alpha particle and the positive nucleus pushed them sharply away. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Chadwick discovers the neutron (1932), explain how it illustrates neutrons and isotopes.
items.answer: Chadwick showed that radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha particles contained neutral particles of about the same mass as the proton. Explained why mass numbers are larger than atomic numbers and made nuclear fission possible.
items.markingKey: Context (Chadwick showed that radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha particles contained neutral particles of about the same mass as the proton.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Explained why mass numbers are larger than atomic numbers and made nuclear fission possible. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to neutrons and isotopes.

items.stem: Tariq plans an investigation into how the angle of deflection affects the number of alpha particles detected, using a computer simulation of the gold-foil experiment. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (detector angle (10°, 30°, 60°, 90°, 150°)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: In alpha decay, how do the mass number and atomic number change?
options: A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2
Both stay the same
A stays the same and Z increases by 1
A decreases by 2 and Z by 4
items.answer: A decreases by 4 and Z decreases by 2
items.markingKey: A. An alpha particle is ⁴₂He.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a background count must be subtracted from count-rate readings.
items.answer: The detector also counts background radiation; subtracting it leaves only the count caused by the source.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The detector also counts background radiation; subtracting it leaves only the count caused by the source. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Ana writes: "Radioactive decay can be sped up by heating the source." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Decay is random and spontaneous; it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical reactions.
items.markingKey: Decay is random and spontaneous; it is not affected by temperature, pressure or chemical reactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Zara is investigating how the thickness of aluminium absorbers affects the count rate from a beta source. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: thickness of aluminium (0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 mm)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: thickness of aluminium (0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 mm) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Sana measured the corrected count rate from a beta source with different thicknesses of aluminium (three 1-minute counts each).

Aluminium thickness / mm | Corrected count rate / counts/min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.0 | 944 | 898 | 913
0.5 | 517 | 514 | 546
1.0 | 293 | 309 | 308
1.5 | 177 | 176 | 180
2.0 | 105 | 103 | 103

Calculate the mean corrected count rate when the aluminium thickness was 1.0 mm.
items.answer: 303.3 counts/min
items.markingKey: M1 (293 + 309 + 308) ÷ 3; A1 303.3 counts/min (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes 3 alpha decays and 2 beta-minus decays. Calculate the mass number and atomic number of the final nucleus.
Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Homes in high-radon areas should be required by law to install radon protection."
items.answer: Mandatory testing with required protection where levels are high balances health and cost.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: radon is a leading cause of lung cancer after smoking; sumps and ventilation are cheap compared with health costs. Arguments against: cost falls on homeowners; risk varies greatly; testing first might be better. Supported judgement: Mandatory testing with required protection where levels are high balances health and cost.

items.stem: Compare the nature, ionising power and penetration of alpha, beta and gamma radiation, and describe an experiment to identify which type(s) a source emits.
items.answer: α: ⁴₂He, +2, highly ionising, stopped by paper / few cm air. β⁻: electron, −1, moderately ionising, stopped by ~3 mm aluminium. γ: EM wave, no charge, weakly ionising, reduced by thick lead. Experiment: measure background; record count rate with source near GM tube; insert paper, then aluminium, then lead; a large drop with paper → α; with aluminium → β; remaining count through Al → γ. Subtract background; handle source with tongs.
items.markingKey: α: ⁴₂He, +2, highly ionising, stopped by paper / few cm air. β⁻: electron, −1, moderately ionising, stopped by ~3 mm aluminium. γ: EM wave, no charge, weakly ionising, reduced by thick lead. Experiment: measure background; record count rate with source near GM tube; insert paper, then aluminium, then lead; a large drop with paper → α; with aluminium → β; remaining count through Al → γ. Subtract background; handle source with tongs.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "background radiation"?
options: Low-level radiation always present, from rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays, food and medical sources
A particle in the nucleus – a proton or a neutron
The joining of two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen isotopes) to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy
A helium nucleus – 2 protons and 2 neutrons, ⁴₂He
items.answer: Low-level radiation always present, from rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays, food and medical sources
items.markingKey: A. "background radiation" is low-level radiation always present, from rocks, radon gas, cosmic rays, food and medical sources.

items.stem: Distinguish between gamma radiation and alpha radiation.
items.answer: Alpha is a helium nucleus, strongly ionising, stopped by paper; gamma is an electromagnetic wave, weakly ionising, reduced only by thick lead or concrete.
items.markingKey: Alpha is a helium nucleus, strongly ionising, stopped by paper; gamma is an electromagnetic wave, weakly ionising, reduced only by thick lead or concrete. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Marie and Pierre Curie (1898) as an example, explain discovery of radioactive elements.
items.answer: The Curies isolated polonium and radium from pitchblende and showed radioactivity was a property of atoms. Marie Curie’s death from aplastic anaemia showed the dangers of radiation before they were understood.
items.markingKey: Context (The Curies isolated polonium and radium from pitchblende and showed radioactivity was a property of atoms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Marie Curie’s death from aplastic anaemia showed the dangers of radiation before they were understood. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to discovery of radioactive elements.

items.stem: Kwame plans an investigation into how the thickness of aluminium absorbers affects the count rate from a beta source. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (thickness of aluminium (0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 mm)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "One decay per second"?
options: random decay
becquerel (Bq)
radioactive tracer
activity
items.answer: becquerel (Bq)
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of becquerel (Bq).

items.stem: Distinguish between the lifetime of a single nucleus and half-life.
items.answer: Half-life is the time for half of a large sample to decay and is constant; the time at which one nucleus decays is random and unpredictable.
items.markingKey: Half-life is the time for half of a large sample to decay and is constant; the time at which one nucleus decays is random and unpredictable. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Half-life halves each time, so the second half-life is shorter." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Half-life is constant for an isotope; each half-life is the same length of time.
items.markingKey: Half-life is constant for an isotope; each half-life is the same length of time. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Diego plans to investigate modelling radioactive decay by throwing dice, to find how the number of dice remaining changes with the number of throws. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: the same starting number of dice (100); fair six-sided dice; the same rule for removing dice; dice thrown in the same tray
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: the same starting number of dice (100) – the model needs a large sample; fair six-sided dice – the decay probability must be 1/6 for each die; the same rule for removing dice – changing the rule changes the “half-life”; dice thrown in the same tray – dice falling out would be miscounted. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem: A wooden tool contains 1/2 of the carbon-14 found in living wood. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5700 years. Estimate the age of the tool, and give one reason the estimate is uncertain.
items.answer: 5700 years
items.markingKey: M1 1/2 = 1 half-lives; A1 1 × 5700 = 5700 years; B1 decay is random / C-14 levels in the atmosphere have varied / contamination.

items.stem: Using Technetium-99m in hospitals as an example, explain choosing half-life for tracers.
items.answer: About 40 million scans a year use Tc-99m, a gamma emitter with a 6-hour half-life produced from molybdenum-99. Supply relies on a few ageing reactors, so shortages affect patients worldwide.
items.markingKey: Context (About 40 million scans a year use Tc-99m, a gamma emitter with a 6-hour half-life produced from molybdenum-99.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Supply relies on a few ageing reactors, so shortages affect patients worldwide. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to choosing half-life for tracers.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Radiocarbon dating gives exact ages for archaeological remains."
items.answer: Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages with stated uncertainty, not exact dates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: based on a constant, well-measured half-life; calibrated against tree rings. Arguments against: decay is random so results have uncertainty (e.g. ±50 years); atmospheric C-14 levels have varied; contamination affects samples. Supported judgement: Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages with stated uncertainty, not exact dates.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by half-life, describe how you would determine it from a set of count-rate readings, and explain how half-life affects the choice of isotope for a medical tracer and for dating rocks.
items.answer: Half-life: time for activity / number of undecayed nuclei to halve. Measure background; record count rate at regular intervals; subtract background; plot corrected count rate against time; read the time for the count to halve from several starting points and average. Tracer: short half-life (hours), gamma emitter → low dose, detectable outside. Dating rocks: half-life comparable with age (e.g. uranium-238, 4.5 billion years) so a measurable fraction remains.
items.markingKey: Half-life: time for activity / number of undecayed nuclei to halve. Measure background; record count rate at regular intervals; subtract background; plot corrected count rate against time; read the time for the count to halve from several starting points and average. Tracer: short half-life (hours), gamma emitter → low dose, detectable outside. Dating rocks: half-life comparable with age (e.g. uranium-238, 4.5 billion years) so a measurable fraction remains.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a long half-life makes nuclear waste difficult to deal with.
items.answer: The waste stays radioactive for thousands of years, so it must be stored safely, isolated from people and groundwater, for a very long time.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The waste stays radioactive for thousands of years, so it must be stored safely, isolated from people and groundwater, for a very long time. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a short half-life source and a long half-life source.
items.answer: A long half-life source has a low, slowly falling activity for a given number of nuclei and stays hazardous for a long time; a short half-life source is very active but its activity falls quickly.
items.markingKey: A long half-life source has a low, slowly falling activity for a given number of nuclei and stays hazardous for a long time; a short half-life source is very active but its activity falls quickly. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Lars recorded the corrected count rate of a protactinium generator over time (three runs).

Time / s | Corrected count rate / counts/10 s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0 | 376 | 385 | 367
60 | 218 | 212 | 218
120 | 112 | 115 | 113
180 | 63 | 63 | 64
240 | 36 | 35 | 34

Calculate the mean corrected count rate when the time was 0 s.
items.answer: 376.0 counts/10 s
items.markingKey: M1 (376 + 385 + 367) ÷ 3; A1 376.0 counts/10 s (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Felix investigated modelling radioactive decay by throwing dice, to find how the number of dice remaining changes with the number of throws. The method had this weakness: with only 100 dice the curve was irregular. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: pool the class’s results so the sample is larger and the randomness averages out
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: pool the class’s results so the sample is larger and the randomness averages out

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "critical mass"?
options: The small decrease in total mass in a nuclear reaction, released as energy (E = mc²)
The minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustaining chain reaction
Using the known half-life of an isotope to find the age of a rock or once-living material
The number of nuclei decaying per second, measured in becquerels (Bq)
items.answer: The minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustaining chain reaction
items.markingKey: B. "critical mass" is the minimum mass of fissile material needed for a self-sustaining chain reaction.

items.stem: A student claims: "Fusion reactors are already producing electricity for the grid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Experiments such as JET and NIF have released fusion energy, but no fusion power station yet supplies the grid.
items.markingKey: Experiments such as JET and NIF have released fusion energy, but no fusion power station yet supplies the grid. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why fission products are a problem for nuclear power.
items.answer: The daughter nuclei are radioactive, often with long half-lives, so spent fuel must be stored securely for thousands of years.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The daughter nuclei are radioactive, often with long half-lives, so spent fuel must be stored securely for thousands of years. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Lars is investigating how the number of neutrons released per fission affects the growth of a chain reaction, using a mousetrap-and-ball (or online) model. Formulate a testable hypothesis and justify it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: If more balls are released per trap, then the number of traps triggered will rise faster, because each event causes more further events – like extra neutrons in fission.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: testable prediction in "if … then …" form linking the independent and dependent variables; 1-2 marks: scientific explanation. Model: If more balls are released per trap, then the number of traps triggered will rise faster, because each event causes more further events – like extra neutrons in fission.

items.stem: Using National Ignition Facility (2022) as an example, explain fusion ignition.
items.answer: Lasers focused on a deuterium–tritium pellet produced more fusion energy (3.15 MJ) than the laser energy delivered (2.05 MJ). A scientific milestone, though the lasers used far more electrical energy than was produced.
items.markingKey: Context (Lasers focused on a deuterium–tritium pellet produced more fusion energy (3.15 MJ) than the laser energy delivered (2.05 MJ).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A scientific milestone, though the lasers used far more electrical energy than was produced. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to fusion ignition.

items.stem: Describe how a nuclear reactor uses fission to generate electricity, including the roles of the fuel, moderator, control rods and coolant, and evaluate nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source.
items.answer: U-235 absorbs a slow neutron → splits into two daughters + 2–3 neutrons + energy; moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons to keep one neutron per fission causing another; coolant carries heat to boiler → steam → turbine → generator. Evaluation: very low CO₂, reliable baseload, small fuel mass; but radioactive waste, high cost and long build time, accident risk (Chernobyl, Fukushima), proliferation concerns. Judgement with reasons.
items.markingKey: U-235 absorbs a slow neutron → splits into two daughters + 2–3 neutrons + energy; moderator slows neutrons; control rods absorb neutrons to keep one neutron per fission causing another; coolant carries heat to boiler → steam → turbine → generator. Evaluation: very low CO₂, reliable baseload, small fuel mass; but radioactive waste, high cost and long build time, accident risk (Chernobyl, Fukushima), proliferation concerns. Judgement with reasons.

items.stem: Why is fusion very difficult to achieve on Earth?
options: Fusion produces no energy
Hydrogen is very rare
Nuclei must be extremely hot and close together to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
Fusion needs uranium
items.answer: Nuclei must be extremely hot and close together to overcome their electrostatic repulsion
items.markingKey: C. Temperatures over 100 million °C.

items.stem: Explain the difference between nuclear fusion and nuclear fission.
items.answer: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one. Both convert a little mass into energy.
items.markingKey: Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one. Both convert a little mass into energy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

State the generation at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 5; range = 19; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 5; 1 range = max − min = 477 − 458 = 19; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Which precaution reduces exposure when handling a source?
items.answer: Using long tongs to increase distance
items.markingKey: Using long tongs to increase distance. Time, distance, shielding.

items.stem: Hana writes: "Food that has been irradiated is radioactive." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Irradiated food is exposed to gamma rays but does not become radioactive.
items.markingKey: Irradiated food is exposed to gamma rays but does not become radioactive. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the distance from a gamma source affects the corrected count rate, to justify using tongs, state the dependent variable and describe how Mateo should measure it.
items.answer: corrected count rate (counts per minute minus background)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: corrected count rate (counts per minute minus background).

items.stem: A worker receives a dose rate of 0.2 μSv per hour above background for 3 hours a day on 220 working days a year. Calculate the extra annual dose in mSv and compare it with the 20 mSv annual limit for radiation workers.
items.answer: 0.132 mSv; well below the 20 mSv limit
items.markingKey: M1 0.2 × 3 × 220 = 132 μSv; A1 0.132 mSv; B1 comparison with 20 mSv.

items.stem: Ingrid investigated how the distance from a gamma source affects the corrected count rate, to justify using tongs. The method had this weakness: the exact position of the source inside its holder was unknown, so distances were slightly wrong. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: plot count rate against 1/(d + x) and find the offset x, or use larger distances
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: plot count rate against 1/(d + x) and find the offset x, or use larger distances

items.stem: Briefly explain why beta sources are used to monitor the thickness of paper in a factory.
items.answer: Beta partly passes through paper; if the paper gets thicker, fewer beta particles reach the detector, so the rollers can be adjusted. Alpha would be fully stopped and gamma would hardly change.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Beta partly passes through paper; if the paper gets thicker, fewer beta particles reach the detector, so the rollers can be adjusted. Alpha would be fully stopped and gamma would hardly change. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Define the term "gamma ray (γ)".
items.answer: High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: high-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from an unstable nucleus. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What fraction of the original nuclei remains after 4 half-lives?
Which model of the atom did the nuclear model replace?
options: The wave model
The plum-pudding model
The quark model
The Bohr model
items.answer: The plum-pudding model
items.markingKey: B. Thomson’s model of positive charge with embedded electrons.

items.stem: Distinguish between control rods and the moderator.
items.answer: Control rods absorb neutrons to slow the rate of reaction; the moderator slows neutrons down so they can cause fission.
items.markingKey: Control rods absorb neutrons to slow the rate of reaction; the moderator slows neutrons down so they can cause fission. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a medical tracer and radiotherapy.
items.answer: Radiotherapy uses a large, targeted dose to kill cancer cells; a tracer uses a small dose of a short-lived gamma emitter to image an organ.
items.markingKey: Radiotherapy uses a large, targeted dose to kill cancer cells; a tracer uses a small dose of a short-lived gamma emitter to image an organ. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between beta-minus decay and alpha decay.
items.answer: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged; in alpha decay A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2.
items.markingKey: In beta-minus decay a neutron becomes a proton, so Z rises by 1 and A is unchanged; in alpha decay A falls by 4 and Z falls by 2. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Half-life halves each time, so the second half-life is shorter." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Half-life is constant for an isotope; each half-life is the same length of time.
items.markingKey: Half-life is constant for an isotope; each half-life is the same length of time. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an atom is electrically neutral overall.
items.answer: It has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so the charges cancel.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It has equal numbers of protons (positive) and electrons (negative), so the charges cancel. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Lars writes: "Fusion reactors are already producing electricity for the grid." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Experiments such as JET and NIF have released fusion energy, but no fusion power station yet supplies the grid.
items.markingKey: Experiments such as JET and NIF have released fusion energy, but no fusion power station yet supplies the grid. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Fukushima Daiichi, Japan (2011) and explain what it reveals about nuclear safety and risk.
items.answer: A tsunami disabled cooling systems, causing meltdowns in three reactors and releases of radioactive material. Few deaths from radiation, but evacuation caused great harm and changed energy policy in Japan and Germany.
items.markingKey: Context (A tsunami disabled cooling systems, causing meltdowns in three reactors and releases of radioactive material.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Few deaths from radiation, but evacuation caused great harm and changed energy policy in Japan and Germany. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to nuclear safety and risk.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Marie and Pierre Curie (1898) shows discovery of radioactive elements.
items.answer: The Curies isolated polonium and radium from pitchblende and showed radioactivity was a property of atoms. Marie Curie’s death from aplastic anaemia showed the dangers of radiation before they were understood.
items.markingKey: Context (The Curies isolated polonium and radium from pitchblende and showed radioactivity was a property of atoms.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Marie Curie’s death from aplastic anaemia showed the dangers of radiation before they were understood. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to discovery of radioactive elements.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Ötzi the Iceman shows radiocarbon dating.
items.answer: Carbon-14 dating of the body found in the Alps in 1991 showed he lived about 5300 years ago. Dating needs a known half-life and an assumed starting ratio of C-14 to C-12.
items.markingKey: Context (Carbon-14 dating of the body found in the Alps in 1991 showed he lived about 5300 years ago.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Dating needs a known half-life and an assumed starting ratio of C-14 to C-12. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to radiocarbon dating.

items.stem: An ion of calcium-40 (^40_20Ca) has a charge of +2. How many protons, neutrons and electrons does it have?
items.answer: 20 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons
items.markingKey: B1 20 protons; B1 20 neutrons; M1 a +2 ion has lost 2 electrons; A1 18 electrons.

items.stem: Uranium-235 (Z = 92) absorbs a neutron and splits into ^141_56Ba and a nucleus with Z = 36, releasing 3 neutrons. Calculate the mass number of the second nucleus.
Using Chernobyl, Ukraine (1986) as an example, explain contamination and its effects.
items.answer: A reactor explosion and fire released radioactive iodine-131 and caesium-137 across Europe; about 350 000 people were relocated. Thyroid cancers increased in children who consumed contaminated milk; the exclusion zone remains today.
items.markingKey: Context (A reactor explosion and fire released radioactive iodine-131 and caesium-137 across Europe; about 350 000 people were relocated.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Thyroid cancers increased in children who consumed contaminated milk; the exclusion zone remains today. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to contamination and its effects.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the thickness of aluminium absorbers affects the count rate from a beta source, state the dependent variable and describe how Rafael should measure it.
items.answer: corrected count rate (counts per minute minus background)
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: corrected count rate (counts per minute minus background).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Radiocarbon dating gives exact ages for archaeological remains."
items.answer: Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages with stated uncertainty, not exact dates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: based on a constant, well-measured half-life; calibrated against tree rings. Arguments against: decay is random so results have uncertainty (e.g. ±50 years); atmospheric C-14 levels have varied; contamination affects samples. Supported judgement: Radiocarbon dating gives reliable ages with stated uncertainty, not exact dates.

items.stem: Describe the alpha-scattering experiment and explain how its results led to the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: Alpha particles from a source fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum; detector moved around. Most went straight through → atom mostly empty space. Some deflected at small angles → positive charge concentrated. A very few bounced back → tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing most of the mass. Electrons orbit at a distance. Replaced plum-pudding model.
items.markingKey: Alpha particles from a source fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum; detector moved around. Most went straight through → atom mostly empty space. Some deflected at small angles → positive charge concentrated. A very few bounced back → tiny, dense, positive nucleus containing most of the mass. Electrons orbit at a distance. Replaced plum-pudding model.

items.stem: "Governments should fund fusion research instead of building new fission power stations." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Fund both: fission for near-term low-carbon power, fusion as a long-term option.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: fusion has no long-lived waste and abundant fuel; no risk of meltdown. Arguments against: fusion power may be decades away; climate action is needed now; fission is proven, low-carbon technology. Supported judgement: Fund both: fission for near-term low-carbon power, fusion as a long-term option. items.stem: Discuss the uses of radioactive isotopes in medicine and industry, explaining how the type of radiation and half-life are chosen for each, and evaluate the risks and how they are managed.
items.answer: Uses: tracers (Tc-99m gamma, 6 h – detectable outside, short dose); radiotherapy (Co-60 gamma, or targeted isotopes); sterilisation (gamma penetrates packaging); thickness gauges (beta, long half-life for steady readings); smoke detectors (alpha, Am-241, 432 years). Risks: DNA damage, cancer; contamination vs irradiation; managed by time–distance–shielding, dosimeters, ALARA, secure storage and disposal. Evaluation of benefits vs risks, judgement.
items.markingKey: Uses: tracers (Tc-99m gamma, 6 h – detectable outside, short dose); radiotherapy (Co-60 gamma, or targeted isotopes); sterilisation (gamma penetrates packaging); thickness gauges (beta, long half-life for steady readings); smoke detectors (alpha, Am-241, 432 years). Risks: DNA damage, cancer; contamination vs irradiation; managed by time–distance–shielding, dosimeters, ALARA, secure storage and disposal. Evaluation of benefits vs risks, judgement.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number of decays detected per second (or minute) by a Geiger–Müller tube"?
options: moderator
background radiation
isotopes
count rate
items.answer: count rate
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of count rate.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "random decay".
items.answer: It is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: it is impossible to predict when a particular nucleus will decay, only the probability. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "isotopes".
items.answer: Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why a chain reaction can occur in uranium-235.
items.answer: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons; if at least one of them causes another fission, the reaction continues.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each fission releases 2 or 3 neutrons; if at least one of them causes another fission, the reaction continues. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Any amount of radiation will definitely cause cancer." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Risk increases with dose; low doses (like background) carry a very small risk.
items.markingKey: Risk increases with dose; low doses (like background) carry a very small risk. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly explain why gamma emission does not change the mass number or atomic number of a nucleus.
items.answer: A gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation with no mass or charge; it only carries away excess energy.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A gamma ray is electromagnetic radiation with no mass or charge; it only carries away excess energy. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a source with a half-life of a few hours would not be suitable for measuring paper thickness in a factory.
items.answer: Its activity would fall quickly, so readings would change through the day and the source would need replacing very often.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Its activity would fall quickly, so readings would change through the day and the source would need replacing very often. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The mass number is the mass of the atom in grams." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The mass number is a count of nucleons; it has no unit.
items.markingKey: The mass number is a count of nucleons; it has no unit. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why fusion is described as a possible “clean” energy source.
items.answer: It produces no CO₂ and no long-lived radioactive fission products; the fuel (deuterium, tritium bred from lithium) is abundant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It produces no CO₂ and no long-lived radioactive fission products; the fuel (deuterium, tritium bred from lithium) is abundant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Freya measured the corrected count rate from a sealed gamma source at different distances (three 1-minute counts each).

Distance from source / cm | Corrected count rate / counts/min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 3246 | 3269 | 3227
15 | 1419 | 1349 | 1349
20 | 758 | 777 | 765
30 | 340 | 342 | 339
40 | 198 | 203 | 198

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The count rate falls rapidly as distance increases – roughly to a quarter when the distance doubles. Gamma rays spread out from the source over the surface of a sphere, so intensity follows an inverse-square law; keeping a distance (tongs) greatly reduces exposure.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The count rate falls rapidly as distance increases – roughly to a quarter when the distance doubles.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Gamma rays spread out from the source over the surface of a sphere, so intensity follows an inverse-square law; keeping a distance (tongs) greatly reduces exposure.

items.stem:
Freya measured the corrected count rate from a beta source with different thicknesses of aluminium (three 1-minute counts each).

Aluminium thickness / mm | Corrected count rate / counts/min: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.0 | 760 | 752 | 718
0.5 | 421 | 414 | 424
1.0 | 238 | 236 | 236
1.5 | 140 | 88 | 137
2.0 | 81 | 84 | 84

Identify the anomalous result. Calculate the mean corrected count rate at 1.5 mm, excluding the anomaly.
items.answer: Anomaly: 88 counts/min (trial 2 at 1.5 mm); mean = 138.5 counts/min
items.markingKey: 1 anomaly identified (88) as it does not fit the pattern of the other repeats; M1 mean of the two remaining values; A1 138.5 counts/min.

items.stem: In an investigation into modelling radioactive decay by throwing dice, to find how the number of dice remaining changes with the number of throws, explain why this control must be applied in the same way in every trial: fair six-sided dice.
items.answer: the decay probability must be 1/6 for each die
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (fair six-sided dice) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: the decay probability must be 1/6 for each die. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden (1909–1911) shows the nuclear model of the atom.
items.answer: Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil: most passed through, a few were deflected, about 1 in 8000 bounced back. An unexpected result led to a new model, showing how evidence changes scientific theories.
items.markingKey: Context (Alpha particles fired at thin gold foil: most passed through, a few were deflected, about 1 in 8000 bounced back.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An unexpected result led to a new model, showing how evidence changes scientific theories. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the nuclear model of the atom.

items.stem: Sofia is investigating how the number of neutrons released per fission affects the growth of a chain reaction, using a mousetrap-and-ball (or online) model. Identify the independent variable in this investigation.
items.answer: number of “neutrons” (balls) released per triggered trap (1, 2, 3)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: number of “neutrons” (balls) released per triggered trap (1, 2, 3) (the variable that is deliberately changed). The measured variable scores 0.

items.stem: A worker receives a dose rate of 0.4 μSv per hour above background for 0.5 hours a day on 200 working days a year. Calculate the extra annual dose in mSv and compare it with the 20 mSv annual limit for radiation workers.
items.answer: 0.04 mSv; well below the 20 mSv limit
items.markingKey: M1 0.4 × 0.5 × 200 = 40 μSv; A1 0.04 mSv; B1 comparison with 20 mSv.

items.stem: Uranium-238 (Z = 92) undergoes 1 alpha decay and 2 beta-minus decays. Calculate the mass number and atomic number of the final nucleus.

Ana plans an investigation into modelling radioactive decay by throwing dice, to find how the number of dice remaining changes with the number of throws. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (throw number (0, 1, 2, … 10)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: "The alpha-scattering experiment proved that the plum-pudding model was completely wrong." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: The experiment disproved the distribution of charge in the plum-pudding model, but science builds on earlier models rather than discarding them completely.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: large-angle deflections could not happen with spread-out charge; the results fitted a nuclear model quantitatively. Arguments against: the model correctly included electrons and overall neutrality; one experiment led to a better model, which was itself later refined (Bohr, neutrons). Supported judgement: The experiment disproved the distribution of charge in the plum-pudding model, but science builds on earlier models rather than discarding them completely. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the number of neutrons released per fission affects the growth of a chain reaction, using a mousetrap-and-ball (or online) model. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Set 50 mousetraps in a clear box, each loaded with 1, 2 or 3 table-tennis balls; drop a single ball in; video the box and count triggered traps in 5 s; repeat three times for each number of balls; compare with a branching-model simulation.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (mousetraps can snap fingers; load them with tongs and wear eye protection). Model: Set 50 mousetraps in a clear box, each loaded with 1, 2 or 3 table-tennis balls; drop a single ball in; video the box and count triggered traps in 5 s; repeat three times for each number of balls; compare with a branching-model simulation.

items.stem: "The benefits of using ionising radiation in medicine outweigh the risks." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Benefits usually greatly outweigh the risks when each use is justified and doses are minimised.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: diagnoses and treats cancers, saving many lives; doses are carefully controlled and kept ALARA. Arguments against: small increase in cancer risk, especially from repeated scans; staff exposure and radioactive waste. Supported judgement: Benefits usually greatly outweigh the risks when each use is justified and doses are minimised.
